stories.headline: World has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11, Pahalgam attacks: India at UN
stories.title: World has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11, Pahalgam attacks: India at UN
stories.summary: United Nations, Oct 8: Exposing Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism at the UN, India has called out Islamabad’s efforts to gloss over its state support for terror by announcing rewards for JeM chief Masood Azahar, underlining that the world has not forgotten 9/11, 26/11 and Pahalgam attacks. India on Wednesday exercised its Right of Reply in response to the Pakistan representative’s statement in the Sixth Committee of the UN General Assembly on the Agenda Item: Measures to Eliminate International Terrorism. “Pakistan speaks of combating terrorism while seeking to obscure the very question that this committee must confront: What happens when terrorists are financed, facilitated, trained, sheltered, or supported from the territory of a state?” First Secretary in the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Raghoo Puri said. He said India has been consistent on this question, underscoring that terrorism cannot be defeated by declarations and instead requires action against its perpetrators, organisers, financiers, and sponsors. “For years, Pakistan has presented itself as a frontline state in combating terrorism and as a victim while masking the fact that the Frankensteins the Pakistani state has created and lost control over have moved from wreaking havoc in neighbouring countries to doing the same in Pakistan,” Puri said. Calling out Pakistan’s doublespeak on terrorism, Puri said the country “glosses over its state support for terrorism by announcing enhanced rewards for apprehending UN-listed head of Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorist and mastermind of several attacks against my country, Masood Azhar.” He said the world is aware of Pakistan’s financial support to terrorism. “Yet, we also remember that just a few months ago, Pakistani representatives used this forum to call the Jaish-e-Mohammed a defunct organisation. The world has seen the script play earlier, and we are clear-eyed that this time also it is going to be no different,” he said. Puri said that when the media can reach Azhar and get confirmation from him about the success of Operation Sindoor, “surely the Pakistani state knows his whereabouts”. In May last year, India had launched Operation Sindoor targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in retaliation for the dastardly April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir perpetrated by The Resistance Front, a proxy of Pakistan-based terror group Lashkar-e-Taiba, in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists were killed. ExploreHistory Earlier this month, India had dismissed as “gimmicks” Pakistan’s fresh announcement of a bounty of seven million rupees on Azhar, demanding that Islamabad take “concrete action” to combat terrorism. India has for years accused Pakistan of sheltering Azhar, while Pakistan has maintained that he fled to Afghanistan – a claim rejected by Afghanistan’s Taliban government. For the last few years, Islamabad has claimed that the JeM founder has been operating from Afghanistan. However, the Taliban regime dismissed Pakistan’s repeated claims, with a senior Afghan Foreign Ministry official saying he is not in the country. Islamabad’s fresh announcement on the reward for information on Azhar came as it faces pressure from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to crack down on terror groups and their leadership. The Paris-based global watchdog is set to review Pakistan’s anti-terrorism efforts at its upcoming plenary. Pakistan was placed under the FATF grey list between 2018 and 2022 for its systemic deficiencies in anti-money laundering and its failure to counter-terror financing. Puri also recalled a recent statement by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, daughter of former Pakistan prime minister Nawaz Sharif, who had said,“The unfortunate thing is that the threat [Punjab] faces comes less from my neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces.” Exposing this “dark secret”, Puri said, “You cannot run with the hares and hunt with the hounds. Reality never works like that.” “When terrorist groups are allowed to operate under state political power, international commitments become meaningless and when perpetrators are provided safe havens, the victims of terrorism are denied justice,” he said. “The world has not forgotten 9/11 and where its perpetrators, including Osama bin Laden, were caught. The world has not forgotten 26/11. The world has not forgotten Pahalgam,” Puri said, adding that the list, “unfortunately”, is painfully long. “The victims in Pahalgam were not asked about their political orientation, they were asked about their religion. It is therefore deeply ironic that Pakistan speaks of combating religious hatred while allowing the conditions that enable it to persist and thrive, especially by fomenting cross-border terrorism,” he said. “Pakistan continues with its narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation. If bombed-out airfields and cratered runways look like victory to Pakistan, they are of course welcome to enjoy it,” Puri said. “Any regime against terrorism to be effective must do two things: assign responsibility and ensure accountability. India will defend its people, and continued terrorism against India will have consequences,” he added. In another Right of Reply, Puri said India rejected Pakistan’s “circular economy” of words and narratives. “If this much effort had actually been made in countering terrorism rather than narrative building, misinformation, and disinformation, the world would have been a better place. But nothing more can be expected from a Form 47 government,” he said, referring to a term used to describe allegations of rigging and manipulation in Pakistan’s 2024 general elections.

stories.headline: Nana Patekar: The actor who stood with soldiers in Kargil, adopted 48 Army schools in J&K
stories.title: Nana Patekar: The actor who stood with soldiers in Kargil, adopted 48 Army schools in J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 08: Veteran actor and filmmaker Nana Patekar, who passed away on Thursday at the age of 75 after suffering a cardiac arrest in Goa, was far more than a cinematic icon for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. He was a man who stood shoulder to shoulder with soldiers in the Kargil war zone, spent nearly two months in the conflict area, and later adopted 48 Army Goodwill Schools across the region, including seven in Ladakh. His demise brings an end to a career spanning nearly five decades, but for the border regions of J&K and Ladakh, his association extended far beyond his film roles. Patekar's connection with Ladakh dates back to the 1999 Kargil conflict. After undergoing extensive military training while preparing for his 1991 film 'Prahaar: The Final Attack', Patekar sought permission to join the Army during the Kargil War. He approached then Defence Minister George Fernandes and was eventually permitted to travel to the conflict zone. Patekar later recalled that he spent around 60 days with Army personnel, travelling through Dras, Leh, Kupwara, Baramulla and Sopore. He also said he became associated with a Quick Reaction Team (QRT). His experience was physically demanding. Patekar recalled that he weighed around 76 kg when he reached Srinagar and returned at about 56 kg after his stint with the troops. That loss of 20 kilograms was a measure of the conditions he endured alongside the soldiers. His connection with Ladakh continued years later through social work. In September 2025, while visiting families affected by Pakistani shelling in Rajouri and Poonch, Patekar said his NGO had adopted 48 Army Goodwill Schools across Jammu and Kashmir, including seven in Ladakh, besides 28 in Kashmir and the remaining schools in Jammu. The initiative was aimed at improving educational standards and infrastructure in the schools. Patekar's NGO 'NAAM' joined hands with the Army in north Kashmir in recent years to develop schools falling close to LoC villages. Nana had said that his experience during the Kargil conflict had left a lasting impression on him. His association with the Army was not merely limited to portraying military characters on screen. Patekar made his Hindi film debut with Gaman in 1978 and went on to deliver acclaimed performances in films including Parinda, Prahaar, Krantiveer, Agni Sakshi, Ab Tak Chhappan, Welcome and Natsamrat. He won three National Film Awards and was awarded the Padma Shri for his contribution to Indian cinema. His preparation for Prahaar included rigorous training with the Maratha Light Infantry, an experience that later became the foundation of his real-life association with the armed forces. Beyond cinema, Patekar was known for his philanthropic work. He co-founded the Naam Foundation with actor Makarand Anaspure and worked extensively with distressed farmers and families affected by drought and other crises. For Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, Nana Patekar's legacy carries an additional dimension. He was not merely an actor who portrayed soldiers on screen. He travelled to the conflict zone, spent time with troops during the Kargil War and, years later, extended his philanthropic work to schools serving children in the border regions. His association with the Army, Kargil and the frontier areas thus remains one of the lesser-known but significant chapters of the life of an actor whose screen presence and off-screen humanitarian work left a lasting imprint on the region.

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026 gold medals for India in Kabaddi, Cricket & Hockey (men & women) is a big statement
stories.title: Asian Games 2026 gold medals for India in Kabaddi, Cricket & Hockey (men & women) is a big statement
stories.summary: FRAGRANCE OF IDEAS Asian Games 2026 came to a glittering conclusion officially on this Sunday, 4th October 2026, in Japan where it started on 19th of September, 2026. It was the 20th edition of the sports extravaganza held in Aichi-Nagoya. The Asian Games 2026 set new records in many games and sports at national, continental and international level. We will in the columns ahead discuss the whole issue from India's perspective and will thus focus mostly on the achievements and missed opportunities of India in the games that lasted for 16 days in Japan -the host nation of the games. In the post-World War II scenario, it was the idea of India to initiate an exercise of Asian Games to bring cordiality in relationships among different nations of the continent. Thus the first Asian Games were held in New Delhi in 1951. Eleven nations participated in the first Asian Games. It was decided at the conclusion of the games to hold them after every four years. By now, the Asian Games have been held in 9 different countries over a period of 75 years. The games were held more than once in some nations including India where they were last organised in 1982. After the break of the USSR in 1991, the five Central Asian nations also joined the Asian Games in 1994 in Hiroshima-Japan and thereby increased the quality and quantity of the continental games. Asia is the biggest continent in the world with the largest population in comparison with the other continents. There are around 50 nations in the continent of Asia. This time 45 nations among them took part in the Asian Games in Japan besides one ‘Asia Refugee Team’ recognised by the Olympics Council of Asia which is responsible for organising the event. A total of 10,787 athletes (with general estimates noting around 11,000 total participants including officials/support staff) took part in the Asian Games 2026. Bad weather in Japan throughout the Games, some mismanagement at different levels by the organisers and the umpiring also became an issue of debate among the sports and media fraternity this time. The Indian contingent in the parade on the occasion of the inauguration of the games was led by Manu Bhakar (Olympics medalist in shooting) and Pawan Sahravat (an icon of Kabaddi). An aggregate of 495 athletes from India took part in this year's Asian Games in Japan. It was notably low as compared to the contingent of 661 athletes that took part in the Asian Games 2022 (held in 2023) in Hangzhou-China. During the games in 2023 in China, the Indian contingent took part in 35 sports and disciplines and brought home 28 gold, 38 silver and 41 bronze aggregating a total of 107 medals -India's biggest number in the Asian Games history. For India, the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games held this year proved to be the second best performance by India in the Asian Games till date. At the conclusion of the Asian Games 2026, India stood again at number 4 on the medal tally after China, Japan and South Korea, the same position which was held by it in the Hangzhou Games. However, the number of medals this time stands at 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze forming a total of 85 medals. In the first week of the Asian Games, there were subdued results coming forth for India, however the results picked up fast in the second week of the Games. While there are some extraordinary achievements and performances for India in these games, there are also some subdued and low-spirited results as well consequent upon underperformances and missed opportunities throughout the duration of the games. Indian athletes won medals across 20 sports disciplines among the 35 disciplines it participated in. Majority of the medals for India came from the following disciplines: Athletics-24, Shooting-15, Archery-9, Wrestling-6, Boxing-6, Squash-5, Nautical sports-3 and Golf-2. Besides the above results, in the games like Cricket, Hockey and Kabaddi, the Indian teams set a new record of winning both men and women gold medals this time. It is for the first time in the history of the Asian Games that India has been able to achieve this kind of a performance that it got the top medals in all these three games (men and women). Historically speaking, Kabaddi, Hockey and Cricket are the grass-root level sports in the whole of South Asia which common people therein have been emotionally attached to and involved in for the last more than one hundred years. These are practically the national games of South Asia, and India has been in the lead most of the time. This time the Indian teams have been successful in demonstrating their prowess and dominance in all these three sports very emphatically at the continental level. Moreover, both the teams of Hockey have also secured quota entry in the ensuing Olympic Games in 2028. In addition to this, among the 21 gold medals India got, Archery contributed 5, Boxing got 3, Shooting-3, wrestling-2, Athletics-1 and Golf-1. It is for the first time that India got a gold medal in golf and the achiever was a young woman athlete, Pranavi Urs. Five women athletes in their solo events won gold medals for India and they included Lovelina Borgohain (Boxing), Parveen Hooda (Boxing), Kumkum Mohod (Archery), Neeru Dhanda (Shooting) besides Pranavi Urs. That the women's events produced 38 medals in a total of 85 medals for India is surely heartening to observe. It exhibits the equal status of women in India and also their emancipation, empowerment and leading role. In athletics, Gulveer Singh, the ace runner, made a hat-trick of medals in the Asian Games this time. His medals included 2 silver (10,000 mtr & 1,500 mtr) and 1 bronze (5,000 mtr). He became the first Indian athlete in 40 years (since the celebrated P.T.Usha) to win three individual medals at a single edition of the Asian Games. His performance spanned middle and long-distance events earning podium finishes from 1,500 mtr to 10,000 mtr events. He had earned a bronze medal in the 10,000 mtr in the last Asian Games in 2023. The gold medal won by a young 17 year old woman athlete, Kumkum Mohod, is overall the 200th gold medal for India in Asian Games history. She signed off India's campaign in Archery in an incredible fashion, becoming the first athlete from the nation to win a Recurve women's individual medal. Her feat in the individual event came after she joined Ankita Bhakat and Kirti to win India's first-ever Recurve women's team gold at the continental event, breaking Korea's historical winning streak of seven consecutive team titles at the Asian Games. Kumkum has also been successful in securing a quota place for the LA28 Olympic Games. During the first week of the games, some disappointing performances by our athletes in the sports like Badminton, Table Tennis, Judo, Swimming, Gymnastics, Karate, Teqball and even Shooting became a cause of worry and concern for the nation. There were some very saddening underperformances as well that failed to boost the medal tally initially. It was in the second week of the games that our athletes lived up to the expectations of the millions of people of the nation. Then there were unfortunately some very close misses at the medal victory points at all the levels and then luck also played its part. However, the achievers lifted everyone's morale and the results came forth with lots of hope, expectations and joy. Here it needs to be noted that China, Japan and South Korea are consecutively at the top three positions of the medal tally of the Asian Games this time also. While China has got an overwhelming 341 medals (169-Gold, 89-Silver & 83-Bronze), Japan got 269 medals (83-Gold, 95-Silver & 91-Bronze) and South Korea confirmed 150 medals (39-Gold, 43-Silver & 68-Bronze). A majority of their medals come from swimming, shooting and athletics. India is practically in a race with Korea and Uzbekistan in the Asian Games who this time are above and below India respectively on the medal tally. India would need a comprehensive overhaul of the sports planning, management, selection process and infrastructure to actually compete at an international level and leave a mark noteworthy of its worth. This is also important keeping in view the ensuing Olympics in 2028 and the centenary Commonwealth Games which are scheduled to be held in India at Ahmedabad in 2030. Any nation in the world is in practical sense viewed by others usually from its civilization, economy, sports, defence and diplomacy. Sports is a well-recognised soft power of a nation besides having its ability to bring people and nations together. India is a leading opinion maker and thought-leader in the world and it is expected that its sports equal its global reputation and recognition. We as a nation need to redouble our efforts to raise our standards in sports for which the government, people and institutions need to come forward effectively and without waste of time. That is the message that our flag-bearer, the shooting champion of the Asian Games 2026 -Neeru Dhanda, brought forward when she was assigned the task of leading the Indian contingent on the occasion of the concluding ceremony of the games with the resolve to meet again in 2030 in Doha-Qatar. (The author is a senior BJP & KP leader, Human Rights Defender and a columnist and can be reached at: ashwanikc2012@gmail.com )

In the first week of the Asian Games, there were subdued results coming forth for India, however the results picked up fast in the second week of the Games.

While there are some extraordinary achievements and performances for India in these games, there are also some subdued and low-spirited results as well consequent upon underperformances and missed opportunities throughout the duration of the games.
Indian athletes won medals across 20 sports disciplines among the 35 disciplines it participated in.
Majority of the medals for India came from the following disciplines: Athletics-24, Shooting-15, Archery-9, Wrestling-6, Boxing-6, Squash-5, Nautical sports-3 and Golf-2.
Besides the above results, in the games like Cricket, Hockey and Kabaddi, the Indian teams set a new record of winning both men and women gold medals this time.
It is for the first time in the history of the Asian Games that India has been able to achieve this kind of a performance that it got the top medals in all these three games (men and women).

Historically speaking, Kabaddi, Hockey and Cricket are the grass-root level sports in the whole of South Asia which common people therein have been emotionally attached to and involved in for the last more than one hundred years.
These are practically the national games of South Asia, and India has been in the lead most of the time.
This time the Indian teams have been successful in demonstrating their prowess and dominance in all these three sports very emphatically at the continental level.
Moreover, both the teams of Hockey have also secured quota entry in the ensuing Olympic Games in 2028.
In addition to this, among the 21 gold medals India got, Archery contributed 5, Boxing got 3, Shooting-3, wrestling-2, Athletics-1 and Golf-1.
It is for the first time that India got a gold medal in golf and the achiever was a young woman athlete, Pranavi Urs.

Five women athletes in their solo events won gold medals for India and they included Lovelina Borgohain (Boxing), Parveen Hooda (Boxing), Kumkum Mohod (Archery), Neeru Dhanda (Shooting) besides Pranavi Urs.
That the women's events produced 38 medals in a total of 85 medals for India is surely heartening to observe.
It exhibits the equal status of women in India and also their emancipation, empowerment and leading role.
In athletics, Gulveer Singh, the ace runner, made a hat-trick of medals in the Asian Games this time.
His medals included 2 silver (10,000 mtr & 1,500 mtr) and 1 bronze (5,000 mtr).
He became the first Indian athlete in 40 years (since the celebrated P.T.Usha) to win three individual medals at a single edition of the Asian Games.
His performance spanned middle and long-distance events earning podium finishes from 1,500 mtr to 10,000 mtr events.
He had earned a bronze medal in the 10,000 mtr in the last Asian Games in 2023.
The gold medal won by a young 17 year old woman athlete, Kumkum Mohod, is overall the 200th gold medal for India in Asian Games history.
She signed off India's campaign in Archery in an incredible fashion, becoming the first athlete from the nation to win a Recurve women's individual medal.

Her feat in the individual event came after she joined Ankita Bhakat and Kirti to win India's first-ever Recurve women's team gold at the continental event, breaking Korea's historical winning streak of seven consecutive team titles at the Asian Games.
Kumkum has also been successful in securing a quota place for the LA28 Olympic Games.

During the first week of the games, some disappointing performances by our athletes in the sports like Badminton, Table Tennis, Judo, Swimming, Gymnastics, Karate, Teqball and even Shooting became a cause of worry and concern for the nation.
There were some very saddening underperformances as well that failed to boost the medal tally initially.
It was in the second week of the games that our athletes lived up to the expectations of the millions of people of the nation.
Then there were unfortunately some very close misses at the medal victory points at all the levels and then luck also played its part.
However, the achievers lifted everyone's morale and the results came forth with lots of hope, expectations and joy.
Here it needs to be noted that China, Japan and South Korea are consecutively at the top three positions of the medal tally of the Asian Games this time also.

While China has got an overwhelming 341 medals (169-Gold, 89-Silver & 83-Bronze), Japan got 269 medals (83-Gold, 95-Silver & 91-Bronze) and South Korea confirmed 150 medals (39-Gold, 43-Silver & 68-Bronze).
A majority of their medals come from swimming, shooting and athletics.
India is practically in a race with Korea and Uzbekistan in the Asian Games who this time are above and below India respectively on the medal tally.

India would need a comprehensive overhaul of the sports planning, management, selection process and infrastructure to actually compete at an international level and leave a mark noteworthy of its worth.
This is also important keeping in view the ensuing Olympics in 2028 and the centenary Commonwealth Games which are scheduled to be held in India at Ahmedabad in 2030.
Any nation in the world is in practical sense viewed by others usually from its civilization, economy, sports, defence and diplomacy.
Sports is a well-recognised soft power of a nation besides having its ability to bring people and nations together.
We as a nation need to redouble our efforts to raise our standards in sports for which the government, people and institutions need to come forward effectively and without waste of time.

That is the message that our flag-bearer, the shooting champion of the Asian Games 2026 -Neeru Dhanda, brought forward when she was assigned the task of leading the Indian contingent on the occasion of the concluding ceremony of the games with the resolve to meet again in 2030 in Doha-Qatar.

stories.title: Flawed by design, exclusionary in impact
stories.summary: The Gyanesh Kumar-led Election Commission of India, emboldened by a deferential Supreme Court judgment, has already disenfranchised lakhs of genuine electors through its Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and risks excluding many more

article_sentences: For more than 75 years, the defining preoccupation of the Election Commission of India (ECI) has been “inclusion”.
The first general election of 1951-52 had to enrol an electorate of around 17 crore from scratch, many of whom were illiterate.
Successive Commissioners treated universal adult franchise as a promise to be fulfilled rather than just a principle to be stated on paper.
India could genuinely be proud of being an electoral democracy where voter turnout among the poor is higher than that among the rich, unlike in many western democracies.
The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls launched by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India, Gyanesh Kumar, has reversed this progressive direction.

It was termed an exercise to “purify” the electoral rolls, but in practice, it is riddled with methodological flaws and ad hoc rule changes, resulting in the deletion of a large number of genuine voters.
The names of 13.37 crore people were struck off during the draft stage across 30 States and Union Territories in the three phases of the SIR.
The figure includes 65 lakh in Bihar, 6.57 crore in the 12 States and Union Territories covered in Phase 2, and 6.15 crore in Phase 3, whose final rolls are yet to be published.
The deletion rate doubled as SIR progressed — from 8.3% in Bihar to 12.9% in Phase 2 and 17% in Phase 3 (it was 32.8% in Delhi and 21.7% in Telangana).
In Phases 1 and 2, even after names were added back, net deletions were about 6.2 crore.
In Delhi, the draft roll has only 97.54 lakh electors, barely above the 94.95 lakh who voted in the February 2025 Assembly election.
In 24 of Delhi’s 70 constituencies, the draft roll now has fewer electors than the number who voted in the election.

stories.headline: Rethinking Progress: Plans, Policies and Projects
stories.title: Rethinking Progress: Plans, Policies and Projects
stories.summary: What does progress mean for Jammu and Kashmir? More roads? More tourists? More hotels and townships? More industrial investment? Higher horticultural production? More construction? All of these can contribute to economic development. Jammu and Kashmir unquestionably needs investment, jobs, higher household incomes, better infrastructure and improved public services. But recent events across the Himalayas increasingly compel us to ask a deeper question: Are the conventional ways in which we define, plan and measure development adequate for a fragile mountain region facing accelerating climatic and ecological change? Dr. R. Balasubramaniam, Member of NITI Aayog, raises precisely this question in his recent article, Rethinking Progress. Reflecting on the devastating August disaster in Nepal and other extreme events, he argues that such tragedies should not simply result in stronger bridges, better warning systems and more disaster-response infrastructure. They should make us examine the assumptions underlying the development model itself. His argument moves beyond conventional sustainability towards what he calls regenerative development: instead of asking only how development can do less environmental damage, we should ask how development can strengthen ecosystems, communities and infrastructure together so that the systems upon which society depends become more resilient rather than progressively depleted. For Jammu and Kashmir, this is an important and timely proposition. From more development to better progress The challenge before J&K is certainly not to choose between development and environmental protection. That is a false choice. The challenge is to ensure that economic development produces durable progress. A road that improves connectivity but greatly increases landslide or flood exposure cannot be judged only by kilometers constructed. Tourism that increases visitor numbers and revenues but overwhelms water supplies, mobility systems, waste infrastructure and fragile landscapes cannot be judged simply by arrivals. Urban expansion that creates valuable real estate while removing drainage channels, wetlands or flood-storage areas may increase today’s asset values while increasing tomorrow’s public liabilities. And agricultural intensification that raises production in the short term but depletes soils, water or ecosystem health may not ultimately increase farmer prosperity. Therefore, the question shifts from how much development are we achieving to what kind of progress is that development producing? That distinction should sit at the center of the next generation of planning in Jammu and Kashmir. Our problem is not the absence of plans J&K does not suffer from a shortage of plans, policies and projects. Tourism has policies and destination-development programs. Agriculture and horticulture have productivity strategies. Urban areas have master plans. Roads, industry, housing, water supply, flood management, forestry and conservation have their own programs and institutional machinery. Most address legitimate needs. The underlying weakness is different: we lack a sufficiently strong common ecological and spatial framework within which these sector plans are designed, reconciled and implemented. Government necessarily works departmentally. Landscapes do not. A forested slope may simultaneously regulate runoff, stabilize soil, store carbon, support biodiversity, provide livelihoods and influence downstream water security. A wetland may look like undeveloped land while performing valuable flood-storage and water-quality functions. Tourism generates employment and income but also generates traffic, water demand, wastewater, solid waste and land-use change. When institutions optimize these objectives independently, individually rational projects can collectively produce irrational outcomes. That is fundamentally a planning-architecture problem. Nature performs infrastructure functions. Forests moderate runoff and erosion. Wetlands absorb and store floodwater. Healthy watersheds protect downstream roads, settlements and reservoirs. Healthy soils store water and sustain agricultural productivity. Urban green systems reduce heat and improve human wellbeing. Balasubramaniam’s call for regenerative development and the Nature-based development planning approach, therefore, converge on an important idea: Progress should leave our economic, social and ecological systems stronger not weaker. For planning purposes, this means designing built and natural infrastructure as complementary parts of the same development system. So, where do we start? Start with the geography that actually connects us Government operates through districts, municipalities, departments and development authorities. Water does not. Floods follow topography. Sediment moves downstream. Forest degradation affects water flows. Urbanization alters runoff. Tourism pressures spill across administrative boundaries. For the Kashmir Valley, the Jhelum River Basin provides an obvious higher-level ecological planning framework. Snow and glaciers, upper catchment forests, springs, tributaries, agriculture, orchards, wetlands, floodplains, Srinagar and Wular are components of one interconnected hydrological system. This does not require another bureaucracy. It requires a nested planning architecture. At the highest level should be J&K’s strategic economic, social and resilience objectives. Basin and landscape planning should establish the underlying resource envelope: water availability, ecological assets, climate and disaster risks, natural infrastructure and broad carrying capacities. Sector strategies for tourism, horticulture, agriculture, forestry, urbanization, transport, industry and energy should then operate within that framework. These strategies should subsequently be differentiated across sub-basins, districts, towns and development-authority areas, while implementation remains with existing departments and agencies. Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) should become standard planning practice Changing the architecture also requires changing our assessment tools. Environmental Impact Assessment, or EIA, generally operates at the individual-project stage. By then, many important strategic decisions—location, development model, scale and investment direction—may already have been made. J&K should, therefore, introduce SEA, as standard good practice for major sector strategies, spatial plans and sub-basin development plans. The difference is significant. An EIA asks: What environmental impacts will this particular road create? An SEA asks: What mobility strategy should this region pursue? Where should new infrastructure go? What alternatives exist? What development will be induced by improved accessibility? And what are the combined consequences for communities, forests, water, climate resilience and disaster risk? Similarly, rather than assessing tourism projects one hotel at a time, an SEA of a destination or tourism strategy would examine its proposed scale and spatial pattern against water availability, waste-management capacity, mobility, ecosystem sensitivity and community needs. Consequently, SEA moves environmental thinking upstream, where fundamental development choices are still open. Look at cumulative impacts, not projects in isolation SEA - Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) are essential planning tools: A single hotel may appear acceptable. So might another. And another. But fifty individually acceptable developments can collectively overwhelm a destination’s roads, water supply, sewage system, waste infrastructure, landscapes and communities. The same applies to roads, hydropower, urban construction and industrial development. Therefore, our planning system needs to ask not merely what each project does, but what all foreseeable development together will do to a landscape or sub-basin. This brings carrying capacity to the center of planning: How much water is sustainably available? How much tourism can a destination accommodate? How much traffic can its road network absorb? How much waste can be treated? How much construction can occur without increasing flood risk? How will these thresholds change under global warming? These are not merely environmental questions. They are questions about the sustainability of economic assets and public investment. Geo-AI can make this practical We also possess capabilities that earlier generations of planners did not. GIS, remote sensing, digital elevation models, hydrological and climate modelling, sensors and artificial intelligence can combine information on forests, wetlands, rivers, glaciers, snow, orchards, settlements, infrastructure, tourism, pollution and hazards. A J&K Geo-AI-enabled planning platform could allow decision-makers to test alternative development scenarios before investments become locked in. What happens to runoff and flood risk? What additional water and energy will be required? What traffic and waste will be generated? Which natural assets will be lost? Which communities benefit and which assume additional risks? Could Nature-based Solutions reduce or complement expensive engineered infrastructure? Technology will not replace political judgement. But it can greatly improve the evidence upon which judgement is exercised. From sustainability towards regeneration J&K already has part of the institutional foundation for this approach. The Jammu and Kashmir Water Resources (Regulation and Management) Act, 2010 calls for planning on a hydrological-unit basis using multidisciplinary approaches and explicitly incorporates basin-master planning. The opportunity is to extend this principle into the wider development-planning architecture. Balasubramaniam’s argument adds another important dimension. Perhaps the objective should no longer be merely to make development less damaging. In particularly fragile landscapes, the ambition should progressively become regenerative: restoring watersheds, strengthening communities, improving soils, rebuilding ecological resilience, and making infrastructure safer while simultaneously expanding livelihoods and economic opportunities. So, what should progress mean for J&K? Jammu and Kashmir must seek economic growth and prosperity. But progress in a Himalayan region should mean more than increasing physical assets and economic transactions. It should mean higher household incomes and productive employment; resilient infrastructure; secure water supplies; healthy forests, wetlands and soils; safer settlements; livable cities; stronger communities; and a natural-resource base capable of supporting future generations. That requires our planning system to move: From measuring development to defining progress; from sectoral optimization to system optimization; from project EIA to Strategic Environmental Assessment; from isolated projects to cumulative-impact assessment; from demand-driven expansion to carrying-capacity-based planning; from remediation after damage to resilience before disaster; and ultimately from merely sustaining depleted systems towards regenerating them. Consequently, the challenge before Jammu and Kashmir policy makers and planners is larger than writing another policy or preparing another master plan. It is to rethink and redo the architecture within which all these plans are made. Dr. Balasubramaniam asks us, in effect, to reconsider what progress itself means. For Jammu and Kashmir, that may be precisely the right place to begin. Development we undoubtedly need. But the real test is whether today’s development leaves tomorrow’s Jammu and Kashmir more prosperous, more resilient and ecologically stronger than we found it. That should be our measure of progress. Javed Hussain Mir, Professor of Practice (Sustainable Development), Islamic University of Science and Technology, Awantipora, Kashmir.

stories.headline: Kashmir’s Vanishing Green Cover: Over 6.6 lakh trees felled in 5 years
stories.title: Kashmir’s Vanishing Green Cover: Over 6.6 lakh trees felled in 5 years
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 8: Kashmir’s tree-felling story is far more extensive than the recent cutting of 14000 Russian poplars. Government records point to lakhs of trees being removed from riverbanks and for infrastructure projects in recent years. The larger question, which remains unasked and unanswered, is: how much green cover has Kashmir lost, and what has actually been restored? Over 5.84 lakh trees were felled along the Jhelum and its associated water channels in five years. This was as per the official Irrigation and Flood Control Department reply to an RTI. The department had identified 6,32,924 trees as encroachments, and chopped down 5,84,153. The largest number of trees, 4,79,074, were identified as encroaching between Panzinara and Banyari, and about 90,000 downstream of Sangam gauge hut at Sampora. There were more- thousands and thousands at other stretches. The felling does not end with the Jhelum. A compliance report filed by the J&K Government before the National Green Tribunal shows that 82,511 trees were felled for 154 infrastructure projects. The compensatory levies remained outstanding, and a total liability of about Rs 49.07 crore was still outstanding. Now, recently, in September, the J&K Government told the Legislative Assembly that 14,255 Russian poplar trees had been felled across seven Kashmir districts in three years. Baramulla had 9,954 of its poplars, followed by Pulwama with 1,648, Anantnag 792, Budgam 754, Srinagar 637, Ganderbal 235 and Kulgam 235. The poplar felling followed restrictions on female Russian poplars. Although the government-constituted committee examining “health issues” related to poplar trees found no established scientific link between poplar pollen and allergies or asthma, yet it assumed that the cotton-like fluff “could” carry dust, fungal spores and pollen and “cause nuisance”. Phased removal of female trees and promotion of male, cotton-free clones was recommended. Illegal logging, encroachment, unauthorised construction, conversion of land and felling of trees on community land are also contributing to loss of green cover. The scale of such loss of trees is harder to quantify; however, the massive change of land-use that Kashmir has seen over the past decade is proof in itself. While the government records trees felled for particular projects or purposes, forest diversion attracts compensatory afforestation. However, there is no readily available record that shows how many mature trees have been felled, how much ecological value was lost, how much compensation was assessed and collected. Government data states that 7.47 crore saplings have been planted under CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority) since 2010. Over 1.06 lakh hectares have been treated through afforestation. However, compensatory afforestation has a survival of 50-60%. As of March 2024, J&K CAMPA had Rs 851.65 crore available, while Rs 727.66 crore remained unutilized. Saplings however, do not replace the value of mature trees. The question, therefore, is not merely how many trees Kashmir is cutting, but whether, apart from felling of trees, the ecological loss is being measured and compensated.

stories.headline: Budgam locals seek new bailey bridge
stories.title: Budgam locals seek new bailey bridge
stories.summary: Budgam, Oct 8: Residents of Kandhama village in Beerwah tehsil of central Kashmir’s Budgam district have urged the government to repair the damaged foundation of the Bailey bridge in the area or replace the ageing structure with a new bridge, citing safety concerns and inconvenience to commuters. Locals said the foundation of the bridge suffered damage during the 2014 floods when flash floods hit the Kashmir Valley. They alleged that the damaged portion has not been repaired by the Roads and Buildings (R&B) Department since then. Showkat Ahmad Mir, a resident of Kandhama, said the foundation of the bridge was damaged around 12 years ago and has continued to deteriorate. “The Bailey bridge was provided during the tenure of the Congress government in Jammu and Kashmir. Earlier, there was a wooden bridge, after which the Indian Army installed this Bailey bridge around 50 years ago. Since then, people have been using this bridge,” Mir said. He said the bridge has already exceeded its prescribed service life and needs urgent attention from the authorities. “The Bailey bridge has already completed its lifespan as per government norms. The structure is not in good condition and could pose a risk to commuters. The damaged foundation has added to the problem,” he said. According to Mir, the bridge is an important link for several areas, connecting villages of Khag tehsil with Baramulla, Beerwah, Magam, Budgam and Srinagar. “If the foundation is not repaired immediately, there is a risk that the bridge could collapse, which may put the lives of people at risk,” he said. Mir urged the government to undertake immediate repairs to the foundation and replace the iron plates of the bridge as a temporary safety measure until a new bridge is constructed. He also expressed concern that many commuters are unaware of the damaged condition of the bridge. “People driving their vehicles over this bridge may not know that its foundation has been damaged. If they were aware of the condition, they might avoid using the bridge until the government carries out the necessary repairs,” Mir said. The residents have appealed to Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha to intervene in the matter and direct the concerned authorities to take immediate measures to ensure the safety of commuters. An official from the R&B Division Beerwah said the department has already submitted a Detailed Project Report (DPR) to the government for construction of a new bridge in the village.
